title: Two Cities
setting: a bike-hire scheme in two cities across a border

post.author: u/rebalance_van_otakar
post.title: I drive the night van for a bike-hire scheme in two cities across a border. At 01:45 the docks in my city forgot every one of our 1,240 members. Over the border, nobody noticed a thing.

blocks.text: I'm Otakar. I drive the night rebalancing van for a bike-hire scheme in two cities across a border: Velmont, in country A, with 1,240 annual members, and Ostravel, in country B, with 860. Bikes stand in docks, racks that keep them locked until a member's card unlocks one. All night I move bikes between docks so mornings start full.

Before unlocking, a dock asks our member system, on computers rented from a cloud company. Each member has a member record: name, payment card, trip history. The cloud company has regions, each a group of its buildings in one area, two per country: A1 and A2 in country A, B1 and B2 in country B.

The live copy of every record sits in A1. For all 2,100 of us, A1 is our home region: the one region holding our records and answering our docks. A question takes 0.3 seconds inside its own country, 0.8 across the border, so Ostravel waits half a second longer. Its contract and country B's law let its records live in A1.
A second copy waits in B1. It's called the standby. Continuous copying keeps it current, in steps: A1 saves a change, sends it across the border, and B1 saves it too, all within seconds.

If A1 fails, B1 takes over, in steps. Every minute a watcher asks A1: are you there? That's a health check. After 5 minutes without an answer, B1 is promoted to live, the docks' questions move to it, and it answers from whatever it holds. Jindra, our engineer, calls that the takeover.

In March a legal review found that country A's data law and Velmont's contract both say Velmont members' records stay in country A. So on Monday 16 March Jindra deleted Velmont's records from B1 and added a filter to the copying: before a change leaves country A, it checks whose record it is and holds back any Velmont member's.
Engineers call a takeover a failover. Our last failover drill, switching A1 off on purpose to watch B1 take over, ran at 04:00 on Tuesday 13 January. B1 held all 2,100. Nothing has failed over since.

Friday 9 October. Velmont's quay bars close at 01:30, so riders come out: about 4 unlocks a minute in Velmont, 2 in Ostravel. At 01:40 A1 went dark, a fault across its whole region; the failed health checks texted Jindra. His log gives time, region and event:

01:40  A1  no answer; checks failing
01:45  A1  silent 5 min; timer runs out
01:45  B1  promoted; docks moved here
01:45  B1  holds Ostravel 860, Velmont 0
01:45  B1  quay dock: unknown member x4

I was refilling the quay dock when four riders came at the van, waving phones. The dock had refused them: unknown member. The app offered each a new sign-up, 60 euros a year. None took it. I opened the admin tablet, our staff screen for the docks: Velmont members: 0. Over the border, Ostravel's 860 rode home.
By 02:15, 124 Velmont unlocks read unknown member. A1 came back at 03:05; Jindra moved the docks back by hand at 03:20. Nothing was lost. B1 had simply never had us.

diagram.aria: Friday night 9 October, 01:30 to 02:15. A1, live for both cities, answers until 01:40, then a regional fault. B1 waits as the standby until 01:45, then is live. Velmont's docks unlock until 01:40, get no answer from 01:40 to 01:45, and from 01:45 every Velmont member is refused as unknown. Ostravel's docks unlock until 01:40, get no answer for the same 5 minutes, then unlock normally from B1. Markers: 01:40 A1's fault, 01:45 the takeover.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from Jindra's log, Friday night 9 October 2026. Green docks unlock; red is every Velmont member refused as unknown. B1 went live at 01:45 holding Ostravel's 860 and none of Velmont's 1,240, so the same takeover that brought Ostravel back left Velmont outside.

blocks.text: Jindra says the copying did exactly what the review asked. What should we change before the next fault?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: One live copy and one waiting copy is called active-passive. A rule about where a person's data may be stored, by law or by contract, is called data residency. So: what did the January drill check, and what has changed in the copying since? At 01:45, which records did B1 hold, and which was it allowed to hold?

replies.author: u/rebalance_van_otakar
replies.text: In January B1 held all 2,100, so it passed. In March the filter went in and Velmont's records came out of B1. At 01:45 it held Ostravel's 860 and none of ours, which is exactly what it's allowed to hold.

comments.author: u/copy_it_all_zelimir
comments.text: A standby that isn't a full copy isn't a standby. Copy every member record to B1 and let the lawyers argue later. That law was written about leaks, not about 1,240 people walking home at two in the morning, and one setting fixes it tonight.

replies.author: u/rebalance_van_otakar
replies.text: Jindra says turning the filter off is one line.

comments.author: u/just_rejoin_kestutis
comments.text: Your app already did the right thing: it offered a sign-up. Waive the 60 euros on takeover nights, let Velmont riders sign up again on the standby, and join the old and new accounts up once A1 is back. Riders ride tonight; you tidy up tomorrow.

reply.prompt: The next region fault could come any night. What should the scheme change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Copy every member record to the standby in B1, so a takeover finds them all.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October Jindra turned the filter off, and every Velmont record began copying to B1 again. In the sim, replaying 9 October: B1 takes over at 01:45 holding Velmont 1,240 of 1,240, and nobody is refused as unknown; 30 riders still get no answer while the timer runs. But 1,240 Velmont records now sit in country B every day, not only on fault nights. On Thursday 5 November the city's yearly data check found them. The city gave the scheme 30 days to delete them or lose the contract, and Jindra switched the filter back on, so the next takeover would find zero again.
options.senior: A takeover can only serve what the standby holds, so filling the standby does fix the night. It does it by breaking the promise the filter was built to keep: a residency rule is about where records are stored every day, not only when they are used, so a copy abroad breaks it whether or not anyone reads it. The fix has to change where the standby is, not what it may hold. Not legal advice: what a rule requires is for the scheme's lawyers.

options.text: Keep the live copy in A1, and add a second standby in A2, inside country A.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October Jindra set up a second standby in A2, copied without the filter because nothing leaves country A. B1 stayed as it was. In the sim, replaying 9 October: at 01:45 A2 takes over holding all 2,100, so nobody is unknown; 30 riders in both cities get no answer while the timer runs, Ostravel's included, because Ostravel's live copy is in A1 too. Ostravel's riders still wait 0.5 seconds more on every unlock, every night. The bill went from 1,400 to 2,100 euros a month: 3 regions, two of them standbys that only wait.
options.senior: Legal and recoverable: every Velmont record stays inside the country whose rule covers it, and a takeover inside country A finds everyone. It keeps active-passive, so one region still serves both cities. Ostravel pays for that in waiting on every unlock, and in going dark whenever A1 does, though nothing in Ostravel failed. And a standby is rent paid on a building that only waits; it is worth it when a long outage costs more than the rent. A fair choice for a small scheme, but not one that keeps each city close to its own records.

options.text: Give each member a home region in their own country, with its standby there too.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October Jindra gave every member a home region in their own country. Velmont's 1,240 stayed in A1, with their standby moved to A2. Ostravel's 860 moved to B1, with a new standby in B2, and their copies in A1 were deleted. Each copying now stays inside one country. In the sim, replaying 9 October: Ostravel never notices, 92 unlocks with no extra wait; Velmont gets no answer for 5 minutes, then A2 takes over at 01:45 holding 1,240 of 1,240. Jindra also made a rule: a drill after every change to the copying. The drill at 04:00 on Tuesday 27 October switched off A1, then B1, and passed both. The bill went from 1,400 to 2,800 euros a month for four regions, and Jindra wrote both numbers into the drill report.
options.senior: A home region per member, inside their own country, turns one active-passive pair into two, one per country, both live at once: active-active, each region serving its own members. A takeover then never has to cross the border, so the residency rule and the recovery plan stop pulling against each other, and a fault in one country touches only that country's riders. The price is four regions instead of two and a routing rule that knows each member's home. And because the copying can change again, a takeover is only proven by a drill run after each change to it.

options.text: Let Velmont members sign up again on the standby, and join their old accounts later.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October Jindra waived the sign-up fee for nights when the standby has taken over. In the sim, replaying 9 October: from 01:45 each of the 124 refused Velmont riders signs up again on B1 and rides. That is 124 duplicate accounts, and 124 new Velmont records in country B, the very thing the filter exists to stop. Their annual passes stayed on their old accounts, so each trip was charged as a single ride. When A1 came back, joining the pairs meant copying records from B1 to A1 by hand and deleting them in B1, and a rider who had used another email or card could not be matched for sure.
options.senior: Signing up again makes a new person, not the old one: a second account with no history, no pass and no link to the first. Every refused rider becomes a duplicate to find and merge later, and each is a new Velmont record created in country B, which breaks the residency rule from the other side. Merging afterwards is the hardest kind of repair, because nothing reliably says two accounts are one person. Keep the original record reachable instead.

sim.title: Replay the takeover night
sim.lede: You're Jindra, replaying Friday night 9 October 2026 from 01:30, one minute at a time. As given data: Velmont has 1,240 annual members and Ostravel 860. The cloud company has two regions in each country, A1 and A2 in country A, B1 and B2 in country B, at about 700 euros a month each, live or standby. As built, every member record is live in A1, and the standby in B1 is kept current by continuous copying; since Monday 16 March the copy filter holds back every Velmont record. Each minute 4 Velmont riders and 2 Ostravel riders, each a different member, try to unlock a bike. A dock's question takes 0.3 seconds inside its own country and 0.8 across the border. At 01:40 A1 has a regional fault. Health checks run every minute; when the takeover timer runs out, the standby is promoted and the docks' questions move to it. Set the design, the copy filter, the fault, the timer and whether refused riders may sign up again, then step a minute at a time or play to 02:15. Run a drill to switch the live region off on purpose and see what the takeover would find.
sim.tryThis: Try this: step to 01:45 as built: B1 is promoted holding Ostravel 860 of 860 and Velmont 0 of 1,240, and the admin tablet reads Velmont members: 0. Play to 02:15: 124 unknown member. Turn the copy filter off: nobody is unknown, and 1,240 Velmont records sit in country B. Set the timer to 1 minute: B1 takes over at 01:41, and 140 are unknown. Sign up again: 124 duplicate accounts. A second standby in A2: everyone found, but Ostravel waits 0.5 s an unlock, for 2,100 euros a month. Home regions: A2 takes over for Velmont with 1,240 of 1,240, Ostravel never notices, 2,800 euros a month. Run a drill as built, then with the filter off, as in January.

explain.oneLine: Nothing lost Velmont's members. The March filter kept their records out of B1, as the law and the city's contract asked, and nobody connected that to the standby. At 01:45 the takeover moved every Velmont dock to a region that had never been allowed to hold them.

steps.title: Active-passive: one live copy, one waiting.
steps.text: As built, the scheme runs active-passive: A1 is live and answers every dock in both cities, and B1 waits as the standby. It is the simplest way to survive losing a region, because only one copy ever takes changes, so the copies never disagree. Its costs: you pay rent on a region that only waits, everyone far from the live region waits on every question (Ostravel's extra 0.5 seconds), and a fault in that one region stops both cities. The other shape is active-active: two regions live at once, each serving some of the members. It works best when each member has one home region that holds their record, so two regions rarely change the same one; Netflix uses the same word, home.

steps.title: The takeover, step by step, and what it cannot move.
steps.text: First, health checks fail: from 01:40 A1 stopped answering. What can go wrong: a slow region looks like a dead one, which is why there is a timer at all. Second, the timer runs out, 5 minutes later, at 01:45. Third, the standby is promoted to live. Fourth, traffic moves: every dock's question now goes to B1. Fifth, B1 answers from what it holds, and nothing else. A failover moves the traffic and the live role; it cannot move records the standby never received. B1 held Ostravel's 860 and none of Velmont's 1,240, so every Velmont member was unknown and the admin tablet counted 0. Measured as RTO, how long until riders could ride, Ostravel's was 5 minutes; measured as RPO, how much data a takeover loses, Velmont's was everything.

steps.title: Residency, the filter, and a drill from January.
steps.text: Data residency is where a person's data may be stored, by law or by contract. Here the rule is country A's own law and the city of Velmont's contract, and both say Velmont members' records stay in country A. The March change did that exactly: it deleted Velmont's records from B1 and filtered the copying. In steps: A1 saves a change; the filter checks whose record it is; a Velmont change stops there; everything else crosses to B1. Nobody asked what that did to the standby. The last drill ran in January, before the filter, when B1 still held all 2,100. A standby that stops matching its primary after a change to the copying is a common pattern, and only a drill after the change finds it before a real fault does.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail.
steps.text: Copying every record to B1 makes the takeover work and breaks the rule every day, not only on fault nights: 1,240 Velmont records sit in country B. A second standby in A2 is the honest trade-off: legal, and everyone is found at 01:45, but Ostravel still waits 0.5 seconds on every unlock, both cities get no answer for 5 minutes whenever A1 fails, and the scheme pays for 3 regions, 2,100 euros a month, two of them only waiting. Letting Velmont riders sign up again on B1 makes 124 duplicate accounts with no passes, and 124 new Velmont records in country B. Shortening the 5-minute timer to 1 minute takes over at 01:41, to the same empty copy: 140 unknown members instead of 124, and more takeovers on a slow minute that was never a fault.

steps.title: Into the other building: B1.
steps.text: On Monday 12 October Otakar parked the van at the quay, and Jindra sat beside him with the tablet pointed at B1 instead of A1: the region across the border that had answered Velmont's docks at 01:45. They went through it row by row. 860 Ostravel members. A filter log that had held back every Velmont change since 16 March. And nothing where 1,240 names had been until 16 March. Nothing in B1 was broken. It had done exactly what it was told, in a building nobody from Velmont had looked into since January.

diagram.aria: The fix: home regions in each country. Velmont's docks ask A1, which is live with Velmont's 1,240 records and copies them to A2, a standby in the same country; if A1 fails, Velmont's docks move to A2. Ostravel's docks ask B1, live with Ostravel's 860 records, copied to B2, a standby in country B. Neither copying crosses the border, so each takeover stays inside its own country.

explain.caption: The fix: every member's home region is in their own country, with its standby in the same country. On 9 October A1 fails, A2 takes over for Velmont with 1,240 of 1,240 at 01:45, and Ostravel, at home in B1, never notices. No copying crosses the border.

fix.title: The fix: a home region for each member in their own country, and a drill after every change to the copying
fix.text: Give every member a home region inside their own country: Velmont's 1,240 live in A1 with their standby in A2; Ostravel's 860 live in B1 with their standby in B2. Each dock asks the member's home region. Both countries are live at once, each serving its own members, so this is active-active by home, and each copying stays inside one country, so a takeover never crosses the border and the filter has nothing left to hold back. Keep the filter anyway, as a guard in case anything is ever pointed across the border again. Then make a drill part of every change to the copying: at a quiet hour, switch each live region off on purpose, check that its standby holds every member it should (1,240 of 1,240, 860 of 860), and write the result down with the date, the time taken and the monthly cost of the regions.

limits: It costs the most: four regions at about 700 euros a month each, 2,800 euros, against 1,400 as built and 2,100 for a second standby in A2. Two of the four only wait. Write that cost beside what a night like 9 October costs the scheme.

A home region is a promise about one member at one moment. A member who moves to the other city is still answered from home, across the border, until someone moves their record, and moving it is a job of its own, checked against the rule first.

Both regions in one country can fail together, from a country-wide network fault or one bad change copied to both, and residency may rule out the usual answer, a copy abroad. Not legal advice: what the rule allows is for the scheme's lawyers.

explain.seniorTake: Before choosing active-passive or active-active, ask two questions of every kind of record: where is it allowed to live, and who must still be served when each region goes dark? Residency decides where copies may sit; recovery decides where a takeover must land; the design has to satisfy both, and the cleanest answer is often a home region per member, inside the country whose rule covers them, with its standby in the same country. Then treat every change to the copying as a change to the recovery plan. A filter, a table left out of the copying, a standby moved to save money: each one quietly changes what a takeover will find, and only a drill after the change shows it. Put the monthly cost of the second region next to the cost of a night without it; that comparison is the decision.

realWorld.title: Netflix, 2016: regional data islands, built for outages
realWorld.text: In Global Cloud: Active-Active and Beyond (Netflix TechBlog, 30 March 2016, read in the Internet Archive), Peter Stout writes: "When we initially launched service in Europe in 2012, we made an explicit decision to build regional data islands for most, but not all, of the member related data." And why: "Since we figured we would have relatively few members travelling across the Atlantic, we felt that the isolation that these data islands created was a win as it would mitigate the impact of a region specific outage." To mitigate is to soften. The islands were built to contain outages, not to obey a law; the post says nothing about residency.

realWorld.title: Netflix: a member's home region
realWorld.text: The same post says an update to a member's recommendations "would only happen if the interaction was serviced in the member's "home" region, or its active-active replica, if any." A replica is a copy. That is this case's idea: each member has one region that holds their data and answers for them, and a copy that can take over.

realWorld.title: Netflix: the islands merged so any region can serve anyone
realWorld.text: The islands carried their own risk: "Our European members, however, were still at risk from a single point of failure." So Netflix changed course: "We decided to create a global cloud where we would be able to serve requests from any member in any AWS region where we are deployed." AWS is Amazon's cloud company. Netflix was free to copy its member data to every region; a scheme bound by a residency rule is not, which is why the fix keeps each country's two regions inside that country.

realWorld.title: Netflix, 2013: the post before
realWorld.text: The 2016 post continues from Netflix's 2013 post, Active-Active for Multi-Regional Resiliency, by Ruslan Meshenberg, Naresh Gopalani and Luke Kosewski (2 December 2013, read in the Internet Archive), which ran two regions live at once. Field Report: Any Region Can Take It reads that post in full; this case only names it.

realWorld.title: GDPR Chapter V: one example of a transfer rule
realWorld.text: Where the European Union's (the EU's) GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, applies, Chapter V, "Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations", Articles 44 to 50, sets conditions for sending personal data out of the EU; a third country is one outside it. Its articles include "General principle for transfers" and "Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision". It is an example of a rule about data leaving a place, not about moving between two EU countries, and it is not the rule in this story. Not legal advice.

realWorld.title: GDPR Article 44
realWorld.text: Article 44 says such a transfer "shall take place only if, subject to the other provisions of this Regulation", the conditions of the Chapter are met, and adds that the Chapter's provisions are applied so that "the level of protection of natural persons guaranteed by this Regulation is not undermined". A natural person is a human being, as opposed to a company. Not legal advice.

realWorld.title: Singapore's PDPA: another example
realWorld.text: Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act, the PDPA, lists a transfer limitation obligation among an organisation's data protection obligations: conditions to meet before personal data is sent out of Singapore. Again an example of a transfer rule, not this story's rule, and not legal advice.

asked: Active-active or active-passive: how do you choose?
How do you serve two regions when some data must stay in one country?
What can a failover not move?
interview.answer: Active-passive means one live copy answers everyone while a standby in another region waits; active-active means two or more regions are live at once, each serving some users, usually the ones whose home region it is. I choose by four things: how long an outage can last, since active-passive needs a takeover and active-active only moves some users; how far users are from the live region, since everyone waits on the far one; whether two regions might change the same record, which active-active must prevent or merge; and cost, since a standby is a region you pay for that only waits. When some data must stay in one country, I start from residency, where each record may live by law or contract, and give each user a home region inside the country whose rule covers them, with its standby in a second region in the same country, so a takeover never crosses the border. A failover in steps: health checks fail, a timer runs out, the standby is promoted, traffic moves, and it serves what it holds. It moves traffic and the live role; it cannot move data the standby never received, such as records a copy filter held back. So I'd drill the takeover after every change to the copying, and write down what each design costs a month. I'd tell the story of a bike-hire scheme whose standby across a border took over holding none of one city's members, because a legal filter had kept them home.

atWork: List every standby or replica your systems would fail over to, and for each ask what has changed in the copying to it since its last failover drill. A standby that stopped matching its primary after a change to the copying (a filter, a table left out, a new field, a moved region) is a common pattern, and it stays hidden until a real fault. On AWS, for a cross-region read replica or a global database, check which tables or rows are excluded from replication and whether the last drill ran after that change. Then write down, for each kind of personal data, where it may live by law or contract, and check that every takeover target is in an allowed place. Build Night tie: L8, The capacity planner, and Build Night N7, Multi-region deploy, capacity and cost, unlock after this case and How Many Machines; for N7, show the monthly cost of a second region (here 1,400 euros as built, 2,100 with a second standby, 2,800 for home regions) and a region-loss drill written up: the date, which region was switched off, what the takeover region held, how long it took, and what changed. Standards, not legal advice: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, an auditor would look under A.5.29 (Information Security During Disruption) and A.5.30 (ICT Readiness for Business Continuity, ICT being information and communications technology) for a takeover plan that is tested, under A.8.14 (Redundancy of Information Processing Facilities) for spare regions that hold what they must, and under A.5.31 (Legal, Statutory, Regulatory and Contractual Requirements) and A.5.34 (Privacy and Protection of PII) for a written record of where each kind of personal data may be stored. For Singapore's DPTM, the PDPA's transfer limitation obligation asks the same question before data leaves Singapore. Build residency into the design and the drill from the first draft, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's app runs from one live database in a European region, with a standby in a United States region kept current by replication. Last quarter a privacy review stopped European Union (EU) customers' personal data from replicating to the US, and their existing copies there were deleted. Your manager asks what happens to EU customers the next time the European region fails, and what you would change.

keyIdeas.idea: The standby holds none of the EU customers, so after the failover they are unknown or missing: a failover serves only what the standby holds
Give each customer a home region inside the place their rule allows, with the standby in a second region there too, so failover never crosses the border
Drill the failover after every change to the replication, and weigh the cost of the extra region

recall.model: The next failover moves EU customers to the US standby, which holds none of their data since the review, so they show up as unknown or as new: a failover serves only what the standby holds, and the filter emptied it for them. Copying their data back would break the review's rule. Instead I'd give each customer a home region inside the place their rule allows: EU customers live in one EU region with their standby in another EU region, so failover never crosses the border, and other customers keep theirs. Then drill the failover after every change to the replication, checking the standby really holds everyone it should, and write down what the extra region costs a month.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with A1 failing at 01:40, which one change lets every Velmont rider unlock from 01:45 without any Velmont record ever sitting in country B?
options: Set the takeover timer to 1 minute
Home regions: Velmont in A1 and A2, Ostravel in B1 and B2
Let refused riders sign up again on the standby
recall.why: With home regions A2 takes over for Velmont at 01:45 holding 1,240 of 1,240, and no copying crosses the border. The filter off finds everyone by keeping 1,240 Velmont records in country B; a 1-minute timer reaches the same empty B1 sooner; signing up again makes 124 new records in country B.

recall.prompt: A failover has run: health checks failed, the timer ran out, the standby was promoted and traffic moved to it. What can it not bring with it?
options: New changes made after the takeover
recall.why: A failover moves traffic and the live role, and the new live copy takes new changes. It cannot move data the standby never got, like Velmont's records held back by the copy filter.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: active-active or active-passive, how do you choose, and how do you serve two regions when some data must stay in one country?

keyIdeas.idea: Active-passive is one live copy and a waiting standby; active-active is several regions live at once, each serving some users
The choice weighs takeover time, distance to the live region, conflicting changes and the cost of an idle region
Residency: a home region per user inside the allowed country, with its standby in a second region of the same country

recall.model: Active-passive is one live copy answering everyone while a standby in another region waits; active-active is two or more regions live at once, each serving some users. I weigh how long a takeover may take, how far users are from the live region, whether two regions could change the same record and how I'd settle a conflict, and what an idle standby costs a month to pay for. When some data must stay in one country, I start from residency: each user gets a home region inside the country whose rule covers them, with its standby in a second region of the same country, so a takeover never crosses the border. Then I drill each takeover after every change to the copying.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Since Monday 19 October each member lives in their own country: Velmont's in A1, with a standby in A2, and Ostravel's in B1, with a standby in B2. Every change to the copying gets a drill. On Saturday 5 December a Velmont annual member moved into a flat in Ostravel and changed her address in the app. Nothing else changed for her. Each time she unlocked a bike in Ostravel, the dock waited 0.8 seconds, not 0.3. On Friday 22 January, at 23:10, A1 had a regional fault, and A2 took over for Velmont at 23:15. For those 5 minutes her dock in Ostravel had no answer, while the Ostravel riders beside her unlocked from B1 as usual.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did she wait, and lose 5 minutes, in a city whose regions never failed, and what should the scheme change?

keyIdeas.idea: Her home region never moved: her record still lives in country A, so every dock she uses asks A1 (or A2) across the border
Moving city should move her home: copy her record to B1 and B2, switch where her docks ask, then delete it from A1 and A2
First check the rule: if Velmont's contract or country A's law still covers her, her record may have to stay, and the wait is its price

coldCase.model: Her home region never moved. A home region is set when a member joins, and changing her address changed nothing about where her record lives, so every dock she uses in Ostravel asks country A across the border: 0.8 seconds instead of 0.3, and on 22 January she waited out A1's 5-minute takeover timer with the rest of Velmont, though B1 was fine. Moving city should move her home: copy her record to B1 and B2, switch which region her docks ask, check it with a drill, then delete it from A1 and A2. But first check the rule with the scheme's lawyers: if she is still a Velmont member under the city's contract, or country A's law still covers her, her record may have to stay in country A, and the wait is the price of the rule. Not legal advice.
